entries.ed4492d4f61db5299973e234360a640f98da1728: <div sID="gen20435" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Mic.4" sID="Mic.4"/> <div eID="gen20435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20436" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20437" type="x-p"/> Comparing this chapter with the close of the foregoing chapter, the comfortable promises here with the terrible threatenings there, we may, with the apostle, "behold the goodness and severity of God," (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.22">Rom. xi. 22</reference>), towards the Jewish church which fell, severity when Zion was ploughed as a field, but towards the Christian church, which was built upon the ruins of it, goodness, great goodness; for it is here promised, I. That it shall be advanced and enlarged by the accession of the nations to it, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. That it shall be protected in tranquility and peace, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.3-Mic.4.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. That it shall be kept close, and constant, and faithful to God, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.5">ver. 5</reference>. IV. That under Christ's government, all its grievances shall be redressed, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.6-Mic.4.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. V. That it shall have an ample and flourishing dominion, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.8">ver. 8</reference>. VI. That its troubles shall be brought to a happy issue at length, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.9-Mic.4.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. VII. That its enemies shall be disquieted, nay, that they shall be destroyed in and by their attempts against it, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.13">ver. 11-13</reference>.
entries.972840c38bc92bf3cd11396945b0c1de1367be00: <div eID="gen20437" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20436" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prosperity of the Church Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 726.)</title> <div sID="gen20438" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But in the last days it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the mountain of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall be established in the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills; and people shall flow unto it. <hi type="super">2</hi> And many nations shall come, and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for the law shall go forth of Zion, and the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from Jerusalem. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he shall judge among many people, and rebuke strong nations afar off; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning-hooks: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more. <hi type="super">4</hi> But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make <hi type="italic">them</hi> afraid: for the mouth of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> For all people will walk every one in the name of his god, and we will walk in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God for ever and ever. <hi type="super">6</hi> In that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , will I assemble her that halteth, and I will gather her that is driven out, and her that I have afflicted; <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will make her that halted a remnant, and her that was cast far off a strong nation: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall reign over them in mount Zion from henceforth, even for ever. <div eID="gen20438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20439" type="x-p"/> It is a very comfortable <hi type="italic">but</hi> with which this chapter begins, and very reviving to those who lay the interests of God's church near their heart and are concerned for the welfare of it. When we sometimes see the corruptions of the church, especially of church-rulers, princes, priests, and prophets, seeking their own things and not the things of God, and when we soon after see the desolations of the church, <hi type="italic">Zion</hi> for their sakes <hi type="italic">ploughed as a field,</hi> we are ready to fear that it will one day perish between both, that the name of Israel shall be no more in remembrance; we are ready to give up all for gone, and to conclude the church will have neither root not branch upon earth. But let not our faith fail in this matter; out of the ashes of the church another phoenix shall arise. In the last words of the foregoing chapter we left <hi type="italic">the mountain of the house</hi> as desolate and waste as the <hi type="italic">high places of the forest;</hi> and is it possible that such a wilderness should ever become a fruitful field again? Yes, the first words of this chapter bring in <hi type="italic">the mountain of the Lord's house</hi> as much dignified by being frequented as ever it had been disgraced by being deserted. Though Zion be ploughed as a field, yet God has not <hi type="italic">cast off his people,</hi> but by the fall of the Jews salvation has come to the Gentiles, so that it proves to be the riches of the world, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.11-Rom.11.12">Rom. xi. 11, 12</reference>. This is the mystery which God by the prophet here shows us, and he says the very same in the <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.3">first three verses</reference> of this chapter which another prophet said by the word of the Lord at the same time (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Isa. ii. 2-4</reference>), that <hi type="italic">out of the mouth of these two witnesses</hi> these promises might be established; and very precious promises they are, relating to the gospel-church, which have been in part accomplished, and will be yet more and more, for he is faithful that has promised. <div eID="gen20439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20440" type="x-p"/> I. That there shall be a church for God set up in the world, after the defection and destruction of the Jewish church, and this in the last days; that is, as some of the rabbin themselves acknowledge, <hi type="italic">in the days of the Messiah.</hi> The people of God shall be incorporated by a new charter, a new spiritual way of worship shall be enacted, and a new institution of offices to attend it; better privileges shall be granted by this new charter, and better provision made for enlarging and establishing the kingdom of God among men than had been made by the Old-Testament constitution: <hi type="italic">The mountain of the house of the Lord</hi> shall again appear firm ground for God's faithful worshippers to stand, and go, and build upon, in their attendance on him, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">v. 1</reference>. And it shall be a centre of unity to them; a church shall be set up in the world, to which the Lord will be daily <hi type="italic">adding such as shall be saved.</hi> <div eID="gen20440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20441" type="x-p"/> II. That this church shall be firmly founded and well-built: It <hi type="italic">shall be established in the top of the mountains;</hi> Christ himself will build it upon a rock; it shall be an impregnable fort upon an immovable foundation, so that the gates of hell shall neither overthrow the one nor undermine the other (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.18">Matt. xvi. 18</reference>); its foundations are still in the <hi type="italic">holy mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.87.1">Ps. lxxxvii. 1</reference>), the <hi type="italic">everlasting mountains,</hi> which cannot, which shall not, be removed. It shall be established, not as the temple, upon one mountain, but upon many; for the foundations of the church, as they are sure, so they are large. <div eID="gen20441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20442" type="x-p"/> III. That it shall be highly advanced, and become eminent and conspicuous: It <hi type="italic">shall be exalted above the hills,</hi> observed with wonder for its growing greatness from small beginnings. The kingdom of Christ shall shine with greater lustre than ever any of the kingdoms of the earth did. It shall be as a <hi type="italic">city on a hill, which cannot be hid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">Matt. v. 14</reference>. The glory of this latter house is greater than that of the former, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag. ii. 9</reference>. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7-2Cor.3.8">2 Cor. iii. 7, 8</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen20442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20443" type="x-p"/> IV. That there shall be a great accession of converts to it and succession of converts in it. <hi type="italic">People shall flow unto it</hi> as the waters of a river are continually flowing; there shall be a constant stream of believers flowing in from all parts into the church, as the people of the Jews flowed into the temple, while it was standing, to worship there. Then many tribes came to the mountain of the house, to enquire of God's temple; but in gospel-times many nations shall flow into the church, shall <hi type="italic">fly like a cloud and as the doves to their windows.</hi> Ministers shall be sent forth to <hi type="italic">disciple all nations,</hi> and they shall not <hi type="italic">labour in vain;</hi> for, multitudes being wrought upon to believe the gospel and embrace the Christian religion, they shall excite and encourage one another, and shall say, "<hi type="italic">Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord</hi> now raised among us, even <hi type="italic">to the house of the God of Jacob,</hi> the spiritual temple which we need not travel far to, for it is brought to our doors and set up in the midst of us." Thus shall people be <hi type="italic">made willing in the day of his power</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>), and shall do what they can to make others willing, as Andrew invited Peter, and Philip Nathanael, to be acquainted with Christ. They shall <hi type="italic">call the people to the mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">Deut. xxxiii. 19</reference>), for there is in Christ enough for all, enough for each. Now observe what it is, 1. Which these converts expect to find in <hi type="italic">the house of the God of Jacob.</hi> They come thither for instruction: "<hi type="italic">He will teach us of his ways,</hi> what is the way in which he would have us to walk with him and in which we may depend upon him to meet us graciously." Note, Where we come to worship God we come to be taught of him. 2. Which they engage to do when they are thus taught of God: <hi type="italic">We will walk in his paths.</hi> Note, Those may comfortably expect that God will teach them who are firmly resolved by his grace to do as they are taught. <div eID="gen20443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20444" type="x-p"/> V. That, in order to this, a new revelation shall be published to the world, on which the church shall be founded, and by which multitudes shall be brought into it: <hi type="italic">For the law shall go forth of Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.</hi> The gospel is here called <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord,</hi> for <hi type="italic">the Lord gave the word, and great was the company of those that published it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.11">Ps. lxviii. 11</reference>. It was of a divine original, a divine authority; it began to be spoken by the Lord Christ himself, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.3">Heb. ii. 3</reference>. And it is <hi type="italic">a law,</hi> a law of faith; we are <hi type="italic">under the law to Christ.</hi> This was to go <hi type="italic">forth from Jerusalem, from Zion,</hi> the metropolis of the Old-Testament dispensation, where the temple, and altars, and oracles were, and whither the Jews went to worship from all parts; thence the gospel must take rise, to show the connexion between the Old Testament and the New, that the gospel is not set up in opposition to the law, but is an explication and illustration of it, and a <hi type="italic">branch growing out of its roots.</hi> It was in Jerusalem that Christ preached and wrought miracles; there he died, rose again, and ascended; there the Spirit was poured out; and those that were to preach repentance and remission of sins to all nations were ordered to <hi type="italic">begin at Jerusalem,</hi> so that thence flowed the streams that were to water the desert world. <div eID="gen20444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20445" type="x-p"/> VI. That a convincing power should go along with the gospel of Christ, in all places where it should be preached (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall judge among many people.</hi> Messiah, the lawgiver (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.2">v. 2</reference>), is here <hi type="italic">the judge,</hi> for to him the Father <hi type="italic">committed all judgment,</hi> and <hi type="italic">for judgment he came into this world;</hi> his word, the <hi type="italic">word of his gospel,</hi> that was to go forth from Jerusalem, was the golden sceptre by which he shall rule and judge when he sits as <hi type="italic">king on the holy hill of Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>. By it he shall <hi type="italic">rebuke strong nations afar off;</hi> for the Spirit working with the word shall <hi type="italic">reprove the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.16.8">John xvi. 8</reference>. It is promised to the Son of David that he shall <hi type="italic">judge among the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.6">Ps. cx. 6</reference>), which he does when in the chariot of his everlasting gospel he goes forth, and goes on, <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer.</hi> <div eID="gen20445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20446" type="x-p"/> VII. That a disposition to mutual peace and love shall be the happy effect of the setting up of the kingdom of the Messiah: <hi type="italic">They shall beat their swords into plough-shares;</hi> that is, angry passionate men, that have been fierce and furious, shall be wonderfully sweetened, and made mild and meek, <reference osisRef="Titus.3.2-Titus.3.3">Tit. iii. 2, 3</reference>. Those who, before their conversion, did injuries, and would bear none, after their conversion can bear injuries, but will do none. As far as the gospel prevails it makes men peaceable, for such is <hi type="italic">the wisdom from above;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">gentle and easy to be entreated;</hi> and if nations were but leavened by it, there would be universal peace. When Christ was born there was universal peace in the Roman empire; those that were first brought into the gospel church were all of <hi type="italic">one heart and of one soul</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.32">Acts iv. 32</reference>); and it was observed of the primitive Christians how well <hi type="italic">they loved one another.</hi> In heaven this will have its full accomplishment. It is promised, 1. That none shall be quarrelsome. The art of war, instead of being improved (which some reckon the glory of a kingdom), shall be forgotten and laid aside as useless. They <hi type="italic">shall not learn war any more</hi> as they have done, for they shall have no need to defend themselves nor any inclination to offend their neighbours. <hi type="italic">Nation shall no longer lift up sword against nation;</hi> not that the gospel will make men cowards, but it will make men peaceable. 2. That all shall be quiet, both from evil and from the fear of evil (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall sit</hi> safely, and none shall disturb them; they shall sit securely, and shall not disturb themselves, every man <hi type="italic">under his vine and under his fig-tree,</hi> enjoying the fruit of them, and needing no other shelter than the leaves of them. <hi type="italic">None shall make them afraid;</hi> not only there shall be nothing that is likely to frighten them, but they shall not be disposed to fear. under the dominion of Christ, as that of Solomon, there shall be <hi type="italic">abundance of peace.</hi> Though his followers have trouble in the world, in him they enjoy great tranquillity. If this seems unlikely, yet we may depend upon it, <hi type="italic">for the mouth of the Lord has spoken it,</hi> and no word of his shall fall to the ground; what he has spoken by his word he will do by his providence and grace. He that is the <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts</hi> will be the <hi type="italic">God of peace;</hi> and those may well be easy whom <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> of all hosts, undertakes the protection of. <div eID="gen20446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20447" type="x-p"/> VIII. That the churches shall be constant in their duty, and so shall make a good use of their tranquillity and shall not provoke the Lord to deprive them of it, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.5">v. 5</reference>. When <hi type="italic">the churches have rest</hi> they shall be edified, and confirmed, and comforted, and shall resolve to be as firm to their God as other nations are to theirs, though they be no gods. Where we find the foregoing promises, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Isa. ii. 2</reference>, &c. it follows (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">O house of Jacob! come ye, and let us walk in the light of the Lord;</hi> and here, <hi type="italic">We will walk in the name of the Lord our God.</hi> Note, Peace is a blessing indeed when it strengthens our resolutions to cleave to the Lord. Observe, 1. How constant other nations were to their gods: <hi type="italic">All people will walk every one in the name of his god,</hi> will own their god and cleave to him, will worship their god and serve him, will depend upon him and put confidence in him. Whatever men make a god of they will make use of, and take his name along with them in all their actions and affairs. The mariners, in a storm, <hi type="italic">cried every man to his god,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.5">Jonah i. 5</reference>. And no instance could be found of a nation's changing its gods, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jer. ii. 11</reference>: If the hosts of heaven were their gods, they loved them, and served them, and <hi type="italic">walked after them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.8.2">Jer. viii. 2</reference>. 2. How constant God's people now resolve to be to him: "<hi type="italic">We will walk in the name of the Lord our God,</hi> will acknowledge him in all our ways, and govern ourselves by a continual regard to him, doing nothing but what we have warrant from him for, and openly professing our relation to him." Observe, Their resolution is peremptory; it is not a thing that needs be disputed: "<hi type="italic">We will walk in the name of the Lord our God.</hi>" It is just and reasonable: He is <hi type="italic">our God.</hi> And it is a resolution for a perpetuity: "We will do it <hi type="italic">for ever and ever,</hi> and will never leave him. He will be ours for ever, and therefore so we will be his, and never repent our choice." <div eID="gen20447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20448" type="x-p"/> IX. That notwithstanding the dispersions, distress, and infirmities of the church, it shall be formed and established, and made very considerable, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.6-Mic.4.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. 1. The state of the church had been low, and weak, and very helpless, in the latter times of the Old Testament, partly through the corruptions of the Jewish nation, and partly through the oppressions under which they groaned. They were like a <hi type="italic">flock of sheep</hi> that were <hi type="italic">maimed, worried,</hi> and <hi type="italic">scattered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.16 ">Ezek. xxxiv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.6 Jer.50.17">Jer. l. 6, 17</reference>. The good people among them, and in other places, that were well inclined, were dispersed, were very infirm, and in a manner lost and cast far off. 2. It is promised that all these grievances shall be redressed and the distemper healed. Christ will come himself (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.24">Matt. xv. 24</reference>), and send his apostles to <hi type="italic">the lost sheep of the house of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.6">Matt. x. 6</reference>. From among the Jews that halted, or that for want of strength, could not go upright, God gathered a remnant (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.7">v. 7</reference>), that <hi type="italic">remnant according to the election of grace</hi> which is spoken of in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7">Rom. xi. 7</reference>, which embraced the gospel of Christ. And from among the Gentiles that were cast far off (so the Gentiles are described to be, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13">Eph. ii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Acts ii. 39</reference>) he raised a strong nation; greater numbers of them were brought into the church than of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.27">Gal. iv. 27</reference>. And such a strong nation the gospel-church is that the gates of hell shall never be able to prevail against it. The church of Christ is more numerous than any other nation, and <hi type="italic">strong in the Lord and in the power of his might.</hi> <div eID="gen20448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20449" type="x-p"/> X. That the <hi type="italic">Messiah</hi> shall be the king of this kingdom, shall protect and govern it, and order all the affairs of it for the best, and this to the end of time. The Lord Jesus <hi type="italic">shall reign over them in Mount Zion</hi> by his word and Spirit in his ordinances, and this <hi type="italic">henceforth and for ever,</hi> for <hi type="italic">of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end.</hi>
entries.b1ebb93d2f2833502efd30dc7c5049caf5ff7675: <div eID="gen20449" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments and Mercies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 726.)</title> <div sID="gen20450" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And thou, O tower of the flock, the strong hold of the daughter of Zion, unto thee shall it come, even the first dominion; the kingdom shall come to the daughter of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">9</hi> Now why dost thou cry out aloud? <hi type="italic">is there</hi> no king in thee? is thy counsellor perished? for pangs have taken thee as a woman in travail. <hi type="super">10</hi> Be in pain, and labour to bring forth, O daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail: for now shalt thou go forth out of the city, and thou shalt dwell in the field, and thou shalt go <hi type="italic">even</hi> to Babylon; there shalt thou be delivered; there the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall redeem thee from the hand of thine enemies. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now also many nations are gathered against thee, that say, Let her be defiled, and let our eye look upon Zion. <hi type="super">12</hi> But they know not the thoughts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , neither understand they his counsel: for he shall gather them as the sheaves into the floor. <hi type="super">13</hi> Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion: for I will make thine horn iron, and I will make thy hoofs brass: and thou shalt beat in pieces many people: and I will consecrate their gain unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth. <div eID="gen20450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20451" type="x-p"/> These verses relate to Zion and Jerusalem, here called the <hi type="italic">tower of the flock</hi> or the <hi type="italic">tower of Edor;</hi> we read of such a place (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.21">Gen. xxxv. 21</reference>) near Bethlehem; and some conjecture it is the same place where the shepherds were keeping their flocks when the angels brought them tidings of the birth of Christ, and some think Bethlehem itself is here spoken of, as <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">ch. v. 2</reference>. Some think it is a tower at that gate of Jerusalem which is called the <hi type="italic">sheep-gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Neh.3.32">Neh. iii. 32</reference>), and conjecture that through that gate Christ rode in triumph into Jerusalem. However, it seems to be put for Jerusalem itself, or for Zion the <hi type="italic">tower of David.</hi> All the sheep of Israel flocked thither three times a year; it was the <hi type="italic">stronghold</hi> (<hi type="italic">Ophel,</hi> which is also a name of a place in Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">Neh. iii. 27</reference>), or castle, of the <hi type="italic">daughter of Zion.</hi> Now here, <div eID="gen20451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20452" type="x-p"/> I. We have a promise of the glories of the spiritual Jerusalem, the gospel-church, which is; the tower of the flock, that one fold in which all the sheep of Christ are protected under one Shepherd: "<hi type="italic">Unto thee shall it come;</hi> that which thou hast long wanted and wished for, <hi type="italic">even the first dominion,</hi> a dignity and power equal to that of David and Solomon, by whom Jerusalem was first raised, that <hi type="italic">kingdom</hi> shall again <hi type="italic">come to the daughter of Jerusalem,</hi> which it was deprived of at the captivity. It shall make as great a figure and shine with as much lustre among the nations, and have as much influence upon them, as ever it had; this is the <hi type="italic">first</hi> or <hi type="italic">chief</hi> dominion." Now this had by no means its accomplishment in Zerubbabel; his was nothing like the first dominion either in respect of splendour and sovereignty at home or the extent of power abroad; and therefore it must refer to the kingdom of the <hi type="italic">Messiah</hi> (and to that the Chaldee-paraphrase refers it) and had its accomplishment when God gave to our Lord Jesus <hi type="italic">the throne of his father David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Luke i. 32</reference>), set him king <hi type="italic">upon the holy hill of Zion</hi> and <hi type="italic">gave him the heathen for his inheritance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">made him, his first-born, higher than the kings of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.89.27">Ps. lxxxix. 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan. vii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">David, in spirit, called him Lord,</hi> and (as Dr. Pocock observes) he witnessed of himself, and his witness was true, that he was greater than Solomon, none of their dominions being like his for extent and duration. The common people welcomed Christ into Jerusalem with <hi type="italic">hosannas to the son of David,</hi> to show that it was the <hi type="italic">first dominion</hi> that came <hi type="italic">to the daughter of Zion;</hi> and the evangelist applies it to the promise of Zion's king coming to her, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.5">Matt. xxi. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zech. ix. 9</reference>. Some give this sense of the words: To Zion, and Jerusalem that tower of the flock, to the nation of the Jews, <hi type="italic">came the first dominion;</hi> that is, there the kingdom of Christ was first set up, the <hi type="italic">gospel of the kingdom</hi> was first <hi type="italic">preached</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Luke xxiv. 47</reference>), there Christ was first called <hi type="italic">king of the Jews.</hi> <div eID="gen20452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20453" type="x-p"/> II. This is illustrated by a prediction of the calamities of the literal Jerusalem, to which some favour and relief should be granted, as a type and figure of what God would do for the gospel-Jerusalem in the last days, notwithstanding its distresses. We have here, <div eID="gen20453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20454" type="x-p"/> 1. Jerusalem put in pain by the providences of God. "She <hi type="italic">cries out aloud,</hi> that all her neighbours may take notice of her griefs, because there is <hi type="italic">no king in her,</hi> none of that honour and power she used to have. Instead of ruling the nations, as she did when she <hi type="italic">sat a queen,</hi> she is ruled by them, and has become a captive. Her <hi type="italic">counsellors</hi> have <hi type="italic">perished;</hi> she is no longer at her own disposal, but is given up to the will of her enemies, and is governed by their counsellors. <hi type="italic">Pangs have taken her.</hi>" (1.) She is carried captive to Babylon, and there is in pangs of grief. "She <hi type="italic">goes forth out of the city,</hi> and is constrained to <hi type="italic">dwell in the field,</hi> exposed to all manner of inconveniences; she <hi type="italic">goes even to Babylon,</hi> and there wears out <hi type="italic">seventy tedious</hi> years in a miserable captivity, all that while <hi type="italic">in pain, as a woman in travail,</hi> waiting to be delivered, and thinking the time very long." (2.) When she is delivered out of Babylon, and redeemed from the hand of her enemies there, yet still she is in pangs of fear; the end of one trouble is but the beginning of another; for <hi type="italic">now also,</hi> when Jerusalem is in the rebuilding, <hi type="italic">many nations are gathered against her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11">v. 11</reference>. They were so in Ezra's and Nehemiah's time, and did all they could to obstruct the building of the temple and the wall. They were so in the time of the Maccabees; they said, <hi type="italic">Let her be defiled;</hi> let her be looked upon as a place polluted with sin, and be forsaken and abandoned both of God and man; let her holy places be profaned and all her honours laid in the dust; <hi type="italic">let our eye look upon Zion,</hi> and please itself with the sight of its ruins, as it is said of Edom (<reference osisRef="Obad.1.12">Obad. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou shouldst not have looked upon the day of thy brother</hi>); let our eyes see our desire upon Zion, the day we have long wished for. When they hear the enemies thus combine against them, and insult over them, no wonder that they are in pain, and cry aloud. <hi type="italic">Without are fightings, within are fears.</hi> <div eID="gen20454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20455" type="x-p"/> 2. Jerusalem made easy by the promises of God: "<hi type="italic">Why dost thou cry out aloud?</hi> Let thy griefs and fears be silenced; indulge not thyself in them, for, though things are bad with thee, they shall end well; thy pangs are great, but they are like those of a <hi type="italic">woman in travail</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.9">v. 9</reference>), that <hi type="italic">labours to bring forth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.10">v. 10</reference>), the issue of which will be good at last." Jerusalem's pangs are not as dying agonies, but as travailing throes, which after a while will be forgotten, for joy that a child is born into the world. Let the literal Jerusalem comfort herself with this, that, whatever straits she may be reduced to, she shall continue until the coming of the Messiah, for there his kingdom must be first set up, and she shall not be destroyed while that blessing is in her; and when at length she is ploughed as a field, and become heaps (as is threatened, <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">ch. iii. 12</reference>), yet her privileges shall be resigned to the spiritual Jerusalem, and in that the promises made to her shall be fulfilled. Let Jerusalem be easy then, for, (1.) Her captivity in Babylon shall have an end, a happy end (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">There shalt thou be delivered, and the Lord shall redeem thee from the hand of thy enemies there.</hi> This was done by Cyrus, who acted therein as God's servant; and that deliverance was typical of our redemption by Jesus Christ, and the release from our spiritual bondage which is proclaimed in the everlasting gospel, that <hi type="italic">acceptable year of the Lord,</hi> in which Christ himself preached <hi type="italic">liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those that were bound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.4.18-Luke.4.19">Luke iv. 18, 19</reference>. (2.) The designs of her enemies against her afterwards shall be baffled, nay, they shall turn upon themselves, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.12-Mic.4.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. They promise themselves a day of it, but it shall prove <hi type="italic">God's day.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">gathered against Zion,</hi> to destroy it, but it shall prove to their own destruction, which Israel and Israel's God shall have the glory of. [1.] Their coming together against Zion shall be the occasion of their ruin. They <hi type="italic">associate themselves, and gird themselves,</hi> that they may break Jerusalem in pieces, but it will prove that they shall be broken in pieces, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa. viii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">They know not the thoughts of the Lord.</hi> When they are gathering together, and Providence favours them in it, they little think what God is designing by it, nor do they understand his counsel; they know what they aim at in coming together, but they know not what God aims at in bringing them together; they aim at Zion's ruin, but God aims at theirs. Note, When men are made use of as instruments of Providence in accomplishing its purposes it is very common for them to intend one thing and for God to intend quite the contrary. The king of Assyria is to be a rod in God's hand for the correction of his people, in order to their reformation; <hi type="italic">howbeit he means not so, nor does his heart think so,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 7</reference>. And thus it is here; the nations are gathered against Zion, as soldiers into the field, but God gathers them <hi type="italic">as sheaves into the floor,</hi> to be beaten to pieces; and they could not have been so easily, so effectually, destroyed, if they had not <hi type="italic">gathered together against Zion.</hi> Note, The designs of enemies for the ruin of the church often prove ruining to themselves; and thereby they prepare themselves for destruction and put themselves in the way of it; they are <hi type="italic">snared in the work of their own hands.</hi> [2.] Zion shall have the honour of being victorious over them, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.13">v. 13</reference>. When they are <hi type="italic">gathered as sheaves into the floor,</hi> to be trodden down, as the corn then was by the oxen, then, "<hi type="italic">Arise, and thresh, O daughter of Zion!</hi> instead of fearing them, and fleeing from them, boldly set upon them, and take the opportunity Providence favours thee with of trampling upon them. Plead not thy own weakness, and that thou art not a match for so many confederated enemies; God will make <hi type="italic">thy horn iron,</hi> to push them down, and <hi type="italic">thy hoofs brass,</hi> to tread upon them when they are down; and thus thou shalt <hi type="italic">beat in pieces many people,</hi> that have long been beating thee in pieces." Thus, when God pleases, <hi type="italic">the daughter of Babylon is made a threshing floor (it is time to thresh her,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">Jer. li. 33</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">worm Jacob</hi> is made <hi type="italic">a threshing instrument,</hi> with which God will <hi type="italic">thresh the mountains, and make them as chaff,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.41.14-Isa.41.15">Isa. xli. 14, 15</reference>. How strangely, how happily, are the tables turned, since Jacob was the threshing-floor and Babylon the threshing instrument! <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa. xxi. 10</reference>. Note, When God has conquering work for his people to do he will furnish them with strength and ability for it, will make the horn iron and the hoofs brass; and, when he does so, they must exert the power he gives them, and execute the commission; even the daughter of Zion must arise, and thresh. [3.] The glory of the victory shall redound to God. Zion shall thresh these sheaves in the floor, but the corn threshed out shall be a meat-offering at God's altar: <hi type="italic">I will consecrate their gain unto the Lord</hi> (that is, I will have it consecrated) and <hi type="italic">their substance unto the Lord of the whole earth.</hi> The spoils gained by Zion's victory shall be brought into the sanctuary, and devoted to God, either in part, as those of Midian (<reference osisRef="Num.31.28">Num. xxxi. 28</reference>), or in whole, as those of Jericho, <reference osisRef="Josh.6.17">Josh. vi. 17</reference>. God is Jehovah, the fountain of being; he is the <hi type="italic">Lord of the whole earth,</hi> the fountain of power; and therefore he needs not any of our gain or substance, but may challenge and demand it all if he please; and with ourselves we must devote all we have to his honour, to be employed as he directs. Thus far all we have must have <hi type="italic">holiness to the Lord</hi> written upon it, all our gain and substance must be <hi type="italic">consecrated to the Lord of the whole earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa. xxiii. 18</reference>. And extraordinary successes call for extraordinary acknowledgments, whether they be of spoils in war or gains in trade. It is God that <hi type="italic">gives us power to get wealth,</hi> which way soever it is honestly got, and therefore he must be honoured with what we get. Some make all this to point at the defeat of Sennacherib when he besieged Jerusalem, others to the destruction of Babylon, others to the successes of the Maccabees; but the learned Dr. Pocock and others think it had its full accomplishment in the spiritual victories obtained by the gospel of Christ over the powers of darkness that fought against it. The nations thought to ruin Christianity in its infancy, but it was victorious over them; those that persisted in their enmity were <hi type="italic">broken to pieces</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Matt. xxi. 44</reference>), particularly the Jewish nation; but multitudes by divine grace were gained to the church, and they and their substance were consecrated to the Lord Jesus, <hi type="italic">the Lord of the whole earth.</hi>  <chapter eID="Mic.4"/> <div eID="gen20455" type="x-p"/>

entries.ec1c2c5d1ac63b5bd63ec8eb90e24e6786f74503: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12756"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.13">Mi 4:1-13</reference>. Transition to the Glory, Peace, Kingdom, and Victory of Zion.</title> <div sID="gen23648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12756"/>1-3. Almost identical with <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Is 2:2-4</reference>.<div eID="gen23648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mountain of the house of the Lord--</hi>which just before (<reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>) had been doomed to be a wild forest height. Under Messiah, its elevation is to be not that of situation, but of moral dignity, as the seat of God's universal empire.<div eID="gen23649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23650" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">people shall flow into it--</hi>In Isaiah it is "all nations": a more universal prophecy. <div eID="gen23650" type="x-p"/>
entries.23f51a3a7b2ceec6b2b656119887ff3bc8ea2828: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12758"/><div sID="gen23653" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12758"/><hi type="bold">4. sit every man under his vine, &c.--</hi>that is, enjoy the most prosperous tranquillity (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.25">1Ki 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.10">Zec 3:10</reference>). The "vine" and "fig tree" are mentioned rather than a house, to signify, there will be no need of a covert; men will be safe even in the fields and open air.<div eID="gen23653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord of hosts hath spoken it--</hi>Therefore it must come to pass, however unlikely now it may seem. <div eID="gen23654" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cef8924155555bd97cc21eda866a9b1211e26f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12759"/><div sID="gen23655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12759"/><hi type="bold">5. For--</hi>rather, Though it be that all people walk after their several gods, yet we (the Jews in the dispersion) will walk in the name of the Lord. So the Hebrew particle means in the Margin, <reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Ge 8:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.13.17">Ex 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.17.18">Jos 17:18</reference>. The resolution of the exile Jews is: As Jehovah gives us hope of so glorious a restoration, notwithstanding the overthrow of our temple and nation, we must in confident reliance on His promise persevere in the true worship of Him, however the nations around, our superiors now in strength and numbers, walk after their gods [Rosenmuller]. As the Jews were thoroughly weaned from idols by the Babylonian captivity, so they shall be completely cured of unbelief by their present long dispersion (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.8-Zech.10.12">Zec 10:8-12</reference>). <div eID="gen23655" type="x-p"/>
entries.bff859d552240c891b97ad2180ced62f6980a93b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12760"/><div sID="gen23656" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12760"/><hi type="bold">6. assemble her that halteth--</hi>feminine for neuter in Hebrew idiom, "whatever halteth": metaphor from sheep wearied out with a journey: all the suffering exiles of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.16">Eze 34:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.19">Zep 3:19</reference>).<div eID="gen23656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">her ... driven out--</hi>all Israel's outcasts. Called "the Lord's flock" (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jr 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.13">Eze 34:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.21">37:21</reference>). <div eID="gen23657" type="x-p"/>
entries.75d5f2556093a07c58a1cc2cffdd0c7212d93c61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12761"/><div sID="gen23658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12761"/><hi type="bold">7. I will make her that halted a remnant--</hi>I will cause a remnant to remain which shall not perish.<div eID="gen23658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord shall reign ... in ... Zion--</hi>David's kingdom shall be restored in the person of Messiah, who is the seed of David and at the same time Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.23">Is 24:23</reference>).<div eID="gen23659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ever--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Da 7:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.33">Lu 1:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>). <div eID="gen23660" type="x-p"/>
entries.71a7d00b33b917e9db5b2d7960d23844a02c793f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12762"/><div sID="gen23661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12762"/><hi type="bold">8. tower of the flock--</hi>following up the metaphor of sheep (see on <reference osisRef="Mic.4.6">Mi 4:6</reference>). Jerusalem is called the "tower," from which the King and Shepherd observes and guards His flock: both the spiritual Jerusalem, the Church now whose tower-like elevation is that of doctrine and practice (<reference osisRef="Song.4.4">So 4:4</reference>, "Thy neck is like the tower of David"), and the literal hereafter (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>). In large pastures it was usual to erect a high wooden tower, so as to oversee the flock. Jerome takes the Hebrew for "flock," Eder or Edar, as a proper name, namely, a village near Beth-lehem, for which it is put, Beth-lehem being taken to represent the royal stock of David (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mi 5:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.35.21">Ge 35:21</reference>). But the explanatory words, "the stronghold of the daughter of Zion," confirm English Version.<div eID="gen23661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stronghold--</hi>Hebrew, "Ophel"; an impregnable height on Mount Zion (<reference osisRef="2Chr.27.3">2Ch 27:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.14">33:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.26">Ne 3:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen23662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto thee shall ... come ... the first dominion--</hi>namely, the dominion formerly exercised by thee shall come back to thee.<div eID="gen23663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kingdom shall come to the daughter of Jerusalem--</hi>rather, "the kingdom of the daughter of Jerusalem shall come (again)"; such as it was under David, before its being weakened by the secession of the ten tribes. <div eID="gen23664" type="x-p"/>
entries.94bd8a25913b6014b89ac85f946abef50ea04024: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12763"/><div sID="gen23665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12763"/>9. Addressed to the daughter of Zion, in her consternation at the approach of the Chaldeans.<div eID="gen23665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is there no king in thee?--</hi>asked tauntingly. There is a king in her; but it is the same as if there were none, so helpless to devise means of escape are he and his counsellors [Maurer]. Or, Zion's pains are because her king is taken away from her (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.9">Jr 52:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.20">La 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>) [Calvin]. The former is perhaps the preferable view (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jr 49:7</reference>). The latter, however, describes better Zion's kingless state during her present long dispersion (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen23666" type="x-p"/>
entries.37b605e14ed9ba402b5afead2eda473032757199: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12764"/><div sID="gen23667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12764"/><hi type="bold">10. Be in pain, and labour--</hi>carrying on the metaphor of a pregnant woman. Thou shalt be affected with bitter sorrows before thy deliverance shall come. I do not forbid thy grieving, but I bring thee consolation. Though God cares for His children, yet they must not expect to be exempt from trouble, but must prepare for it.<div eID="gen23667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go forth out of the city--</hi>on its capture. So "come out" is used <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2Ki 24:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.36.16">Is 36:16</reference>.<div eID="gen23668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwell in the field--</hi>namely, in the open country, defenseless, instead of their fortified city. Beside the Chebar (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.1">Psa 137:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.15">Eze 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen23669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Babylon--</hi>Like Isaiah, Micah looks beyond the existing Assyrian dynasty to the Babylonian, and to Judah's captivity under it, and restoration (<reference osisRef="Isa.39.7">Is 39:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.14">43:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">48:20</reference>). Had they been, as rationalists represent, merely sagacious politicians, they would have restricted their prophecies to the sphere of the existing Assyrian dynasty. But their seeing into the far-off future of Babylon's subsequent supremacy, and Judah's connection with her, proves them to be inspired prophets.<div eID="gen23670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there ... there--</hi>emphatic repetition. The very scene of thy calamities is to be the scene of thy deliverance. In the midst of enemies, where all hope seems cut off, there shall Cyrus, the deliverer, appear (compare <reference osisRef="Judg.14.14">Jud 14:14</reference>). Cyrus again being the type of the greater Deliverer, who shall finally restore Israel. <div eID="gen23671" type="x-p"/>
entries.10f2f4dc63dd366217a82102e7d1d1cfe37e26ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12765"/><div sID="gen23672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12765"/><hi type="bold">11. many nations--</hi>the subject peoples composing Babylon's armies: and also Edom, Ammon, &c., who exulted in Judah's fall (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.16">La 2:16</reference>; Ob 11-13).<div eID="gen23672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">defiled--</hi>metaphor from a virgin. Let her be defiled (that is, outraged by violence and bloodshed), and let our eye gaze insultingly on her shame and sorrow (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.10">Mi 7:10</reference>). Her foes desired to feast their eyes on her calamities. <div eID="gen23673" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3ae01ef4988deb50bb4c084f53ea0806677f1ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12766"/><div sID="gen23674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12766"/><hi type="bold">12. thoughts of the Lord--</hi>Their unsearchable wisdom, overruling seeming disaster to the final good of His people, is the very ground on which the restoration of Israel hereafter (of which the restoration from Babylon is a type) is based in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.8">Is 55:8</reference>; compare with <reference osisRef="Mic.4.3">Mi 4:3</reference>, 12, 13, which prove that Israel, not merely the Christian Church, is the ultimate subject of the prophecy; also in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.13">Ro 11:13</reference>. God's counsel is to discipline His people for a time with the foe as a scourge; and then to destroy the foe by the hands of His people.<div eID="gen23674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gather them as ... sheaves--</hi>them who "gathered" themselves for Zion's destruction (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.11">Mi 4:11</reference>) the Lord "shall gather" for destruction by Zion (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.13">Mi 4:13</reference>), like sheaves gathered to be threshed (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Is 21:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.33">Jr 51:33</reference>). The Hebrew is singular, "sheaf." However great the numbers of the foe, they are all but as one sheaf ready to be threshed [Calvin]. Threshing was done by treading with the feet: hence the propriety of the image for treading under foot and breaking asunder the foe. <div eID="gen23675" type="x-p"/>
entries.8508e0f420f405d2b6e62f69b458597cec42284b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12767"/><div sID="gen23676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12767"/><hi type="bold">13. thresh--</hi>destroy thy foes "gathered" by Jehovah as "sheaves" (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.15">Is 41:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen23676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thine horn--</hi>Zion being compared to an ox treading corn, and an ox's strength lying in the horns, her strength is implied by giving her a horn of iron (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.11">1Ki 22:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beat in pieces many--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>).<div eID="gen23678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will consecrate their gain unto the Lord--</hi>God subjects the nations to Zion, not for her own selfish aggrandizement, but for His glory (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.6">Is 60:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.20">Zec 14:20</reference>, with which compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Is 23:18</reference>) and for their ultimate good; therefore He is here called, not merely God of Israel, but "Lord of the whole earth." <chapter eID="Mic.4"/>

entries.2668f23ddab758dd92baeddb1e0620d5986eec33: <div eID="gen34786" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen34787" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34788" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34788" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34787" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34789" type="x-p"/> In the commencement of this chapter we have a glorious prophecy of the establishment and prosperity of the Messiah's kingdom; its peaceful character, increasing spiritual and political influence, ultimate universality, and everlasting duration, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.4">Mic 4:1-4</reference>. Then breaks in a chorus of his people declaring their peculiar happiness in being members of his kingdom, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.5">Mic 4:5</reference>. The prophet resumes the subject; predicts the restoration and future prosperity of Israel, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.6-Mic.4.8">Mic 4:6-8</reference>; and exhorts them not to be discouraged at their approaching captivity, as they should in due time not only be delivered from it, but likewise be victorious over all their enemies, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.9-Mic.4.13">Mic 4:9-13</reference>. These last verses, which evidently contain a prediction of the final triumph of Christianity over every adversary, have been applied to the conquests of the Maccabees; but the character and beneficial results of their military exploits, as far as we have any account of them, correspond but in a very faint degree to the beautiful and highly wrought terms of the prophecy. The first three verses of this chapter are very similar to the commencement of the second chapter of Isaiah; and the fourth, for beauty of imagery and elegance of expression, is not unworthy of that prophet. <div eID="gen34789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34790" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34791" type="x-p"/> But in the last days it shall come to pass - These four verses contain, says Bp. Newcome, a prophecy that was to be fulfilled by the coming of the Messiah, when the Gentiles were to be admitted into covenant with God, and the apostles were to preach the Gospel, beginning at Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Luk.24.47">Luk 24:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.2.14">Act 2:14</reference>, etc., when Christ was to be the spiritual Judge and King of many people, was to convince many nations of their errors and vices, and was to found a religion which had the strongest tendency to promote peace. Bp. Lowth thinks that "Micah took this passage from Isaiah;" or the Spirit may have inspired both prophets with this prediction; or both may have copied some common original, the words of a prophet well known at that time. The variations (few and of little importance) may be seen in the notes on the parallel passages, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Isa 2:2</reference>, etc.; to which the reader is requested to refer.
entries.be43a84263a4b253dfb4250ed94f5e07b27dc083: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34792" type="x-p"/> Under his vine and under his fig tree - A proverbial expression, indicative of perfect peace, security, and rural comfort. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.2.1">Isa 2:1</reference> (note). This verse is an addition to the prophecy as it stands in Isaiah. See Clarke on <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">Mic 4:1</reference> (note).
entries.8c25275419f234ed0b471545cd38b2678e7f1218: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34793" type="x-p"/> Every one in the name of his god - This shall be the state of the Gentile world; but after the captivity, the Jews walked in the name of Jehovah alone; and acknowledge no other object of religious worship to the present day.
entries.2343ebc1084c9db8044d533029cfd2241cdf54fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34794" type="x-p"/> Will I assemble her that halteth - driven out - afflicted - Under these epithets, the state of the Jews, who were to be gathered into the Christian Church, is pointed out. They halted between the true God and idols; they were driven out into captivity, because of this idolatry; and they were variously afflicted, because they would not return unto the Lord that bought them.
entries.7328d607bd8fa2f80a085b7c0f885898e0aaa0c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34795" type="x-p"/> Her that halted a remnant - I will preserve them as a distinct people after their return from captivity, for the farther purposes of my grace and mercy. <div eID="gen34795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34796" type="x-p"/> And the Lord shall reign over them in Mount Zion - The Chaldee is remarkable here, and positively applies the words to the Messiah: "But thou, O Messiah, of Israel, who art hidden because of the sins of the congregation of Zion, the kingdom shall come unto thee."
entries.69138530d8e96ff4e6b46945c1712223be83c212: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34797" type="x-p"/> O tower of the flock - I think the temple is meant, or Jerusalem; the place where the flock, the whole congregation of the people assembled to worship God. Newcome retains the Hebrew word עדר eder, a tower in or near Beth-lehem, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.21">Gen 35:21</reference> or, as some think, a tower near the sheep-gate in Jerusalem, I believe Jerusalem, or the temple, or both, are meant; for these were considered the stronghold of the daughter-of Zion, the fortress of the Jewish people. <div eID="gen34797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34798" type="x-p"/> Even the first dominion - What was this? The Divine theocracy under Jesus Christ; this former, this first dominion, was to be restored. Hence the angel called him Immanuel, God with us, ruling among us.
entries.290fafbc2a6ed861eba4be79a20224479b7338db: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34799" type="x-p"/> Is there no King in thee? - None. And why? Because thou hast rejected Jehovah thy king. <div eID="gen34799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34800" type="x-p"/> Is thy counsellor perished? - No: but thou hast rejected the words and advices of the prophets. <div eID="gen34800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34801" type="x-p"/> Pangs have taken thee - He is speaking of the desolations that should take place when the Chaldeans should come against the city; and hence he says, "Thou shalt go to Babylon;" ye shall be cast out of your own land, and sent slaves to a foreign country, He represents the people under the notion of a woman in travail.
entries.2b0f1c9874d372d6fdcc5414fe0636a744a297fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34802" type="x-p"/> There shalt thou be delivered - There God shall meet thee; and by redeeming thee from thy captivity, bringing thee back to thine own land, and finally converting thee unto himself, shall deliver thee from the burden of grief and wo which thou now bearest, and under which thou dost groan.
entries.cc421251a164b8f32258d0b63a836f32b70e3ce9: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen34802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34803" type="x-p"/> Many nations are gathered against thee - The Chaldeans, who were composed of many nations. And, we may add, all the surrounding nations were their enemies; and rejoiced when the Chaldean army had overthrown Jerusalem, destroyed the temple, and led the people away captive. <div eID="gen34803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34804" type="x-p"/> Let her be defiled - This was their cry and their wish: Let Jerusalem be laid as low as she can be, like a thing defiled and cast away with abhorrence; that their eyes might look upon Zion with scorn, contempt, and exultation.
entries.b0463761063ce5854aeca889338e54e36424901e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen34804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34805" type="x-p"/> But they know not the thoughts of the Lord - These think that God has utterly rejected his people, and they shall have a troublesome neighbor no more: but this is not his design; he will afflict them for a time; but these, the enemies of his people, he will gather as sheaves into the threshing-floor, there to be trodden, and the wheel to go over them. This is the counsel, the purpose of God, which these do not understand. The persons here referred to are not only the Chaldeans which were threshed by the Persians and Medes; but the Idumeans, Ammonites, Moabites, and Philistines, which the Jews afterwards subdued.
entries.f831f4dfd6b34fdf5e19c7830c87449729b69583: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen34805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34806" type="x-p"/> Arise and thresh, O daughter of Zion - This refers to the subject of the preceding verse. When God shall have gathered together all thy enemies, as into the threshing-floor, he will give thee commission and power to get a complete victory over them, and reduce them to servitude. And that thou mayest be able to do this, he will be on thy side as a powerful helper; here signified by the metaphors, iron horns, and brazen hoofs. Thou shalt have power, authority, and unconquerable strength; for thine enemies shall be no more against thee than the corn against oxen shod with brass, or a puny animal against the horn of a fierce bull tipped with iron. <div eID="gen34806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34807" type="x-p"/> I will consecrate their gain unto the Lord - What they have taken from thee in the way of spoil shall be restored; and again consecrated unto the service of him who will show himself to be the Lord, the Supreme Governor of the whole earth. Was not this prediction fulfilled when Cyrus gave the Jews permission to return to their own land, and gave them back the sacred vessels of the temple which Nebuchadnezzar had carried away? The Maccabees and their successors recovered much of the booty of which the neighboring nations had deprived the Jews; and the treasure taken was devoted to Jehovah. The first verse of the next chapter should conclude this.  <chapter eID="Mic.4"/> <div eID="gen34807" type="x-p"/>

entries.7d39463663dae56ce6ab95dd67fc41d15c55ed1a: Mic 4:1-4 <div eID="gen16555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16556" type="x-p"/> The promise of salvation opens, in closest connection with the destruction of Jerusalem and of the temple, with a picture of the glory awaiting in the remotest future the temple mountain, which has now become a wild forest-height. Mic 4:1. <hi type="italic">“And it comes to pass at the end of the days, that the mountain of Jehovah’s house will be established on the head of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills, and nations stream to it.</hi> Mic 4:2. <hi type="italic">And many nations go, and say, Up, let us go up to the mountain of Jehovah, and to the house of the God of Jacob, that He may teach us of His ways, and we may walk in His paths: for from Zion will law go forth, and the word of Jehovah from Jerusalem.</hi> Mic 4:3. <hi type="italic">And He will judge between many nations, and pronounce sentence on strong nations afar off; and they forge their swords into coulters, and their spears into pruning-hooks: nation will not lift up sword against nation, nor will they learn war any more.</hi> Mic 4:4. <hi type="italic">And they will sit, every one under his vine, and under his fig-tree, and no one will make them afraid: for the mouth of Jehovah of hosts hath spoken it.”</hi><note placement="foot">This promise is placed by Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Isa 2:2-4</reference>) at the head of his prophecy of Zion’s way through judgment from the false glory to the true. The originality of the passage in Micah is open to no question. Delitzsch acknowledges this, and has given the principal arguments in its favour in the <hi type="italic">Commentary on Isaiah</hi>. For still more elaborate proofs, see Caspari’s <hi type="italic">Micha</hi>, pp. 444-5.</note> <div eID="gen16556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16557" type="x-p"/> By the phrase “at the end of the days,” which always denotes the Messianic era when used by the prophets (see at Hos 3:5), the predicted exaltation of the temple mountain is assigned to the period of the completion of the kingdom of God. The mountain of the house of Jehovah is the temple mountain, strictly speaking, Moriah, as the distinction made between the mountain of the house and Zion in Mic 3:12 clearly shows; but as a subordinate peak of Zion, it is embraced along with Zion in what follows (compare Mic 4:2 with Mic 4:7) as the seat of Jehovah’s rule, from which the law proceeds. נכון does not mean placed or set up, but established, founded. By connecting the participle with יהיה, the founding is designated as a permanent one. בּראשׁ ההרים, upon (not at) the top of the mountains, as in Jdg 9:7; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.13">1Sa 26:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.16">Psa 72:16</reference>; whereas such passages as Mic 2:13; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.7">Amo 6:7</reference>, and 1Ki 21:9 are of a different character, and have no bearing upon the point. The temple mountain, or Zion, will be so exalted above all the mountains and hills, that it will appear to be founded upon the top of the mountains. This exaltation is of course not a physical one, as Hofmann, Drechsler, and several of the Rabbins suppose, but a spiritual (ethical) elevation above all the mountains. This is obvious from Mic 4:2, according to which Zion will tower above all the mountains, because the law of the Lord issues from it. The assumption of a physical elevation cannot be established from <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.2">Eze 40:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rev.21.10">Rev 21:10</reference>, for in the visions described in both these passages the earthly elevation is a symbol of a spiritual one. “Through a new revelation of the Lord, which is made upon it, and which leaves the older revelations far behind, whether made upon Sinai or upon itself, Zion becomes the greatest and loftiest mountain in the world” (Caspari), and the mountain seen from afar, to which “nations” stream, and not merely the one nation of Israel. עמּים is more precisely defined in Mic 4:2 as גּוים רבּים. The attractive power which this mountain exerts upon the nations, so that they call upon one another to go up to it (Mic 4:2), does not reside in its height, which towers above that of all other mountains, but in the fact that the house of the God of Jacob stands upon it, i.e., that Jehovah is enthroned there, and teacher how to walk in His ways. הורה מן, to teach out of the ways, so that the ways of God form the material from which they derive continual instruction. The desire for salvation, therefore, is the motive which prompts them to this pilgrimage; for they desire instruction in the ways of the Lord, that they may walk in them. The ways of Jehovah are the ways which God takes in His dealing with men, and by which men are led by Him; in reality, therefore, the ordinances of salvation which He has revealed in His word, the knowledge and observance of which secure life and blessedness. The words “for the law goes forth from Zion,” etc., are words spoken not by the nations, but by the prophet, and assign the reason why the heathen go with such zeal to the mountain of Jehovah. The accent is laid upon מצּיון (from Zion), which stands at the head, and מירוּשׁלם (from Jerusalem), which is parallel to it. Thence does <hi type="italic">tōrâh</hi>, i.e., instruction in the ways of God, proceed, - in other words, the law as the rule of a godly life, and <hi type="italic">debhar Yehōvâh</hi> (the word of Jehovah), or the word of revelation as the source of salvation. It is evident from this that the mountain of the house of God is not thought of here as the place of worship, but as the scene of divine revelation, the centre of the kingdom of God. Zion is the source of the law and word of the Lord, from which the nations draw instruction how to walk in the ways of God, to make it their own, take it to their homes, and walk according to it. The fruit of this adoption of the word of the Lord will be, that they will not longer fight out their disputes with weapons of war, but let Jehovah judge and settle them, and thus acknowledge Him as their King and Judge. שׁפם signifies to act as judge; הוכיה (lit., to set right), to settle and put a stop to a dispute. “Many nations,” in contrast with the one nation, which formerly was alone in acknowledge Jehovah as its King and Judge. This is strengthened still further by the parallel “strong, mighty nations afar off.” In consequence of this they will turn their weapons into instruments of peaceful agriculture, and wage no more war; in fact, they will learn war no more, no longer exercise themselves in the use of arms. For the words וכתּתוּ וגו compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.10">Joe 3:10</reference>, where the summons to the nations to a decisive conflict with the kingdom of God is described as turning the instruments of agriculture into weapons of war. With the cessation of war, universal peace will ensue, and Israel will have no further enemies to fear, so that every one will have undisturbed enjoyment of the blessings of peace, of which Israel had had a foretaste during the peaceful reign of Solomon. The words “sit under his vine” are taken from 1Ki 5:5 (cf. Zec 3:10), and אין מחריד from the promise in Lev 26:6. All this, however incredible it might appear, not only for the Israel of that time, but even now under the Christian dispensation, will assuredly take place, for the mouth of Jehovah the true God has spoken it.
entries.c54deb695fc8fb31b949719c120be3d9a4f86584: Mic 4:5 <div eID="gen16557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16558" type="x-p"/> It will not be through any general humanitarian ideas and efforts, however, that the human race will reach this goal, but solely through the omnipotence and faithfulness of the Lord. The reason assigned for the promise points to this. Mic 4:5. <hi type="italic">“For all nations walk every man in the name of his God, but we walk in the name of Jehovah our God for ever and ever.”</hi> This verse does not contain an exhortation, or a resolution to walk in the name of God, which involves an exhortation, in the sense of “if all nations walk, etc., then we will,” etc.; for an admonition or a resolution neither suits the connection, in the midst of simple promises, nor the words themselves, since we should at any rate expect נלכה instead of נלך. The sameness in the form of the verbs ילכוּ and נלך requires that they should be understood in the same way. Walking in the name of God does not mean regulating the conduct according to the name of a God, i.e., according to the nature which expresses itself in the name, or worshipping him in a manner corresponding to his nature (Caspari), but walking in the strength of God, in which the nature of this God is displayed. This is the meaning of the phrase in <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.45">1Sa 17:45</reference> and Zec 10:12, where “I strengthen them in Jehovah” forms the basis of “and in His name will they walk” (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Pro 18:10</reference>, “The name of the Lord is a strong tower”). But the gods of all the nations, i.e., of all the heathen, are worthless beings, without life, without strength. Jehovah, on the contrary, is the only true God, the almighty Creator and Governor of the world. And the heathen, with their worthless gods, can do nothing to Him and the nation which walks in His name, his strength. If, therefore, Israel rejoices for ever and ever in the strength of its God, the heathen nations cannot disturb the peace which He will create for Israel and all who accept His word. In this way is the promise in Mic 4:3 and Mic 4:4 explained in Mic 4:5. But this explanation assumes that, even at the time when many nations stream to the mountain of the Lord, there will still be nations that do not seek Jehovah and His word, - a thought which is still further expanded in v. Mic 5:4., and involves this consolation, that such opponents of the people of God as shall be still in existence will not be able to interfere with the salvation which has been prepared for it by its God.
entries.50918857783b739c1d28f6d8a9d436433f45c446: Mic 4:6-7 <div eID="gen16558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16559" type="x-p"/> From this salvation even the Israel that may be in misery or scattered abroad will not be excluded. Mic 4:6. <hi type="italic">“In that day, is the saying of Jehovah, will I assemble that which limps, and gather together that which has been thrust out, and which I have afflicted.</hi> Mic 4:7. <hi type="italic">And I will make that which limps into a remnant, and that which is far removed into a strong nation; and Jehovah will rule over them from henceforth, even for ever.” </hi>“In that day” points back to the end of the days in Mic 4:1. At the time when many nations shall go on pilgrimage to the highly exalted mountain of the Lord, and therefore Zion-Jerusalem will not only be restored, but greatly glorified, the Lord will assemble that which limps and is scattered abroad. The feminines הצּלעה and הנּדּחה are neuters, and to be understood collectively. Limping denotes the miserable condition into which the dispersed have been brought (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.35.15">Psa 35:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.18">Psa 38:18</reference>). And this misery is inflicted by God. The limping and dispersed are those whom Jehovah has afflicted, whom He has punished for their sins. The gathering together of the nation has already been promised in Mic 2:12; but there the assembling of all Israel was foretold, whereas here it is merely the assembling of the miserable, and of those who are scattered far and wide. There is no discrepancy in these two promises. The difference may easily be explained from the different tendencies of the two addressed. “All Jacob” referred to the two separate kingdoms into which the nation was divided in the time of the prophet, viz., Israel and Judah, and it was distinctly mentioned there, because the banishment of both had been foretold. This antithesis falls into the background here; and, on the other hand, prominence is given, in connection with what precedes, to the idea of happiness in the enjoyment of the blessings of the holy land. The gathering together involves reinstatement in the possession and enjoyment of these blessings. Hence only the miserable and dispersed are mentioned, to express the thought that no one is to be excluded from the salvation which the Lord will bestow upon His people in the future, though now he may be pining in the misery of the exile inflicted upon them. But just as the whole of the nation of Israel to be gathered together, according to Mic 2:12, consists of the remnant of the nation only, so does the gathering together referred to here point only to the restoration of the remnant, which is to become a strong nation, over which Jehovah reigns as King in Zion. מלך is emphatic, expressing the setting up of the perfected monarchy, as it has never yet existed, either in the present or the past.<note placement="foot">“Micah does not mention the descendants of David here, but Jehovah Himself, not to exclude the kingdom of David, but to show that God will prove that He was the author of that kingdom, and that all the power is His. For although God governed the ancient people by the hand of David, and by the hand of Josiah and Hezekiah, yet there was as it were a cloud interposed, so that God then reigned obscurely. The prophet therefore indicates a certain difference here between that shadowy kingdom and the new kingdom which God will openly manifest at the advent of the Messiah.” - Calvin.</note> <div eID="gen16559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16560" type="x-p"/> This dominion will never be interrupted again, as it formerly was, by the banishment of the nation into exile on account of its sins, but will endure מעתּה (henceforth), i.e., from the future, which is regarded as present, even for ever. <div eID="gen16560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16561" type="x-p"/> So far as the realization of this exceedingly glorious promise is concerned, the expression standing at the head, <hi type="italic">be'achărı̄th hayyâmı̄m</hi> (at the end of the days), already points to the Messianic times: and the substance of the promise itself points to the times of the completion of the Messianic kingdom, i.e., to the establishment of the kingdom of glory (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mat 19:28</reference>). The temple mountain is a type of the kingdom of God in its New Testament form, which is described by all the prophets after the forms of the Old Testament kingdom of God. Accordingly, the going of the nations to the mountain of the house of Jehovah is, as a matter of fact, the entrance of the heathen who have been brought to the faith into the kingdom of Christ. This commenced with the spread of the gospel among the Gentiles, and has been continued through all the ages of the Christian church. But however many nations have hitherto entered into the Christian church, the time has not yet come for them to be so entirely pervaded with the spirit of Christ, as to allow their disputes to be settled by the Lord as their King, or to renounce war, and live in everlasting peace. Even for Israel the time has not yet come for the limping and exiled to be gathered together and made into a strong nation, however many individual Jews have already found salvation and peace within the bosom of the Christian church. The cessation of war and establishment of eternal peace can only take place after the destruction of all the ungodly powers on earth, at the return of Christ to judgment and for the perfecting of His kingdom. But even then, when, according to Rom 11:25., the <hi type="italic">pleroma</hi> of the Gentiles shall have entered into the kingdom of God, and Israel as a nation (πᾶς Ἰσραήλ = יעקב כּלּו in Mic 2:12) shall have turned to its Redeemer, and shall be assembled or saved, no physical elevation of the mountain of Zion will ensue, nor any restoration of the temple in Jerusalem, or return of the dispersed of Israel to Palestine. The kingdom of glory will be set up on the new earth, in the Jerusalem which was shown to the holy seer on Patmos in the Spirit, on a great and lofty mountain (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.10">Rev 21:10</reference>). In this holy city of God there will be no temple, “for the Lord, the Almighty God, and the Lamb, are the temple thereof” (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.22">Rev 21:22</reference>). The word of the Lord to the Samaritan woman concerning the time when men would neither worship God on this mountain, nor yet in Jerusalem, but worship Him in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:21, Joh 4:23), applies not only to the kingdom of God in its temporal development into the Christian church, but also to the time of the completion of the kingdom of God in glory.
entries.24cd13a6311c083c5c31addb09c89ead949aa5b5: Mic 4:8 <div eID="gen16561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16562" type="x-p"/> The prophecy turns from the highest glorification of Zion to the throne of Zion, which had been founded by David, and swept away with the destruction of Jerusalem (Mic 3:12), and predicts its restoration in the future.
